planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring after the last frost in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun; like standard Celeste, Improved Celeste fruits on second-year wood and on new growth late in the season, so avoid heavy winter pruning that removes developing fruit buds.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to sandy soil in full sun, and mulch around the root zone to help protect against winter root injury in the northern part of its range. Improved Celeste is a selection of the classic Celeste fig chosen by growers for producing noticeably larger fruit than the standard cultivar while retaining Celeste's honey-sweet, rose-pink flesh and thin, violet-brown skin, along with its reputation for exceptional cold hardiness and dependable, heavy production in Deep South gardens. It ripens over the same mid-July through August window as standard Celeste and requires the same minimal care — established trees rarely need fertilizer and produce well without spraying. As with all Celeste-type figs, the small, closed eye at the base of the fruit helps deter souring insects and fruit spoilage common in open-eyed fig varieties in humid climates.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — fig variety trials

common_name: Rat-Tail Radish (Podding Radish Grown for Seed Pods)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, spacing seeds further apart than root radishes since this type is grown for its long, sprawling seed pods rather than a swollen root. In zone 9, sow spring through early summer; it tolerates heat far better than standard radishes, which bolt and turn bitter.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun, and provide support or extra spacing as plants grow tall and sprawling. Rat-Tail Radish is an unusual radish type grown not for its root, which stays thin and woody, but for its long, slender, crunchy seed pods that can reach 6–12 inches, twisting into a shape resembling a rat's tail as they mature, best picked young and tender while still snappable between the fingers. The pods carry a peppery radish bite and are eaten raw in salads, pickled, or stir-fried, and unlike root radishes the plant thrives in hot weather without turning bitter or woody, making it a productive summer crop when standard radishes have long since bolted. Harvest continuously to encourage more pod production, since pods left to mature and dry stop the plant from setting new ones.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Rat-Tail Radish variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Co. — Asian vegetable seed catalog

common_name: Chinese Flowering Kale (Yod Fah, Flowering Gai Lan)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or, better, in fall for a winter crop in mild climates, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese flowering kale is grown specifically to flower and is intentionally allowed to bolt for harvest, unlike most brassicas.

directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin seedlings to allow strong flowering stalks to develop. Known in Thai and Southeast Asian markets as yod fah ('flower tip'), Chinese flowering kale is a gai lan (Chinese broccoli) type grown specifically for its tender, slightly sweet flowering stems, harvested with the small buds still tightly closed or just beginning to open, rather than for leaves or heads as with most brassicas. Stems, leaves, and unopened flower buds are all edible with a mild, cabbage-broccoli flavor and pleasant crunch, commonly stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce. Harvest the main flowering stalk when buds are plump but unopened, which encourages side shoots to develop for a continued harvest over several weeks; plants that are allowed to fully flower and set seed turn tough and bitter.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Co. — Asian vegetable seed catalog

University of California Cooperative Extension — Asian vegetable production guide

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Komatsuna develops its deepest purple-red color in cool weather and with strong light, fading toward green in hot summer conditions or deep shade.

directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin to final spacing for full-sized rosettes or grow tightly spaced for a cut-and-come-again baby-leaf harvest. Red Komatsuna is a purple-red-leaved selection of komatsuna, the fast-growing, cold-hardy Japanese mustard spinach, offering the same tender, mild, slightly mustardy flavor as the standard green form but in leaves flushed deep maroon-purple, especially vivid in cool fall and winter growing conditions. It is a productive, quick-maturing green well suited to a fall or early-spring planting, tolerating light frost better than true spinach while adding striking color contrast to salad mixes and stir-fries. Harvest whole young plants or pick individual outer leaves for a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest, since the plant regrows readily from the crown after cutting.

common_name: Walking Stick Cabbage (Jersey Cabbage, Jersey Kale)

planting.note: Direct sow or start transplants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Walking Stick Cabbage is grown over a long season to develop its tall, thick stalk, so give it a permanent, undisturbed spot for the better part of a year.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking young plants in windy sites and stripping lower leaves as they yellow to encourage the tall, straight stalk this heirloom is famous for. Walking Stick Cabbage, also called Jersey cabbage or Jersey kale, is a historic giant kale from the Channel Islands traditionally grown for two purposes at once: the young leaves are edible and used as livestock fodder or cooked greens, while the plant is left to grow over a full season into a remarkably tall, woody stalk that was traditionally dried, straightened, and varnished into walking sticks and canes, a cottage tradition dating back centuries on Jersey. In the vegetable garden it makes an unusual, dramatic vertical accent as well as a productive source of greens over many months, tolerating poor soil and coastal conditions well. Harvest lower leaves continuously through the growing season for eating, and let a stalk mature untouched at season's end if canes are wanted.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — heirloom brassica notes
